title: While loops
summary: Repeat code for as long as a condition holds, and keep reading input until the user is done.

steps.title: Repeat while a condition is true
body: An `if` runs its block once. A `while` runs its block **again and again**, for as long as the condition stays true.
prints `1`, `2`, `3`. Each trip through the block is called a **pass**:
1. Check the condition. If it is false, jump past the closing brace.
Something inside the block must eventually make the condition false. Delete `count++` and this loop never ends: an **infinite loop**.

steps.explain: `n` goes 1, 3, 9, 27. The condition is only checked at the top of each pass, so the loop stops the first time `n` is 20 or more, and by then it is already 27.

steps.explain: Print first, then count down. Swap those two lines and the output becomes `2`, `1`, `0`.

steps.title: do-while: run first, ask later
body: A `while` checks its condition **before** the first pass, so the block may never run at all. Sometimes you need it to run at least once, for example to show a menu before asking whether to show it again.
This prints `100` once, even though `100 < 3` was never true. Note the `;` after the condition: a `do`-`while` is the only loop that ends with one.

steps.prompt: How many times does the block run?
steps.explain: The block runs before the condition is ever checked. After one pass `x` is 11, `11 < 5` is false, and the loop ends.

steps.title: break and continue
body: Two keywords change course in the middle of a pass.
- `break;` leaves the loop **now**. Execution carries on after the closing brace.
- `continue;` abandons the **rest of this pass** and goes back to check the condition.

prints `1`, `2`, `4`, `5`. `while (true)` looks like an infinite loop, and it would be without the `break`. It is a common shape when the natural place to decide "are we done?" is in the middle of the block.
> **Tip:** change the counter **before** a `continue`. If `n++` came after it, `n` would stay at 3 forever.

steps.explain: `Write` keeps everything on one line. 1 is printed, 2 is skipped by `continue`, 3 and 4 are printed, and at 5 the `break` ends the loop before anything is written.

steps.title: Loops driven by input
body: Loops are how a program handles input of **unknown length**. The usual trick is a **sentinel**: a special value that means "that was the last one".
Here `0` is the sentinel. The read appears twice: once before the loop, once at the end of each pass. Forget the second one and the loop spins on the same number forever.

steps.explain: Keep going *while* the number is *not* the sentinel. `+=` adds to the total; a plain `=` would throw away everything added so far.

prompt: Read lines until one of them is `stop`. Count and add up the whole numbers. Lines that are not whole numbers (words, blank lines) are **skipped**.
Then print the count and the sum. For the input
starter: // Loop: read a line, leave on "stop", skip lines that are not numbers
hints: `while (true)` with one `Console.ReadLine()` at the top of the block is the easiest shape here.
Check for `"stop"` first and `break`. Then use `int.TryParse(line, out int n)`: it returns `false` when the line is not a whole number.
`if (!int.TryParse(line, out int n)) continue;` skips the bad line. After it, `count++` and `sum += n`.
